549d2cd86c.q: What are the primary functions of a manufacturing data platform that monitors production in real-time?
549d2cd86c.a: The platform helps manufacturing companies answer simple questions like when they will finish a job and where it is at in real-time, giving managers and operators fingertips access to data rather than relying on paper. It also helps with improvement projects by providing data to manufacturing engineers to understand where problems are, fix them, monitor progress over time, and sustain those gains.

84c79c95f0.q: How did a manufacturing software company pivot from targeting machine OEMs to end-user manufacturers?
84c79c95f0.a: The company started by trying to help mid-market machine manufacturers monitor their equipment in the field with a software-enabled services model, but found that machine manufacturers were not ready for this approach. They pivoted in 2016 toward end users, connecting directly to factory floor equipment via PLCs and sensors, and eventually developed a comprehensive platform to manage entire factory operations.

b5368d573a.q: What percentage of manufacturing equipment today lacks modern PLC network connectivity?
b5368d573a.a: In 2024, Bryan estimates that maybe 30 to 40 percent of the equipment they touch is PLC connected and on the network. The majority of manufacturing equipment is really old and does not have PLCs, which required the company to develop hardware kits to collect data rather than relying on direct connections.
b5368d573a.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

fb483f0599.q: What was the key turning point that accelerated growth for a manufacturing IoT platform?
fb483f0599.a: The turning point was creating a turnkey solution from a single vendor that could get data from machines, pump it to the cloud, and provide dashboards and user interfaces all from one customer, so manufacturers did not have to deal with six different people to get it set up. This took until 2019 to achieve and provided fast implementation and ease of use.

be61dbc3af.q: How does the technology adoption curve framework apply to implementing manufacturing systems?
be61dbc3af.a: The adoption curve labels different groups: early adopters who are technology enthusiasts and tolerate product issues, then an early majority who want turnkey solutions and will not tolerate problems. These patterns hold true inside organizations too, with different groups having different comfort levels with new technology, requiring strategies to drag all personalities along during implementation.
be61dbc3af.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

680342f27c.q: What is the key to operator adoption of manufacturing data entry systems on the shop floor?
680342f27c.a: The system should require only two button clicks to do 90% of what operators need to do, with automated delivery of data to other people so operators do not have to change their workflow. Instead of entering data into a system, operators can use a simple interface while automation handles data distribution, minimizing disruption to their primary job of making parts.
680342f27c.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

c9b1ea545b.q: What unique skill set is required for manufacturing IoT system administrators?
c9b1ea545b.a: Administrators need networking knowledge to work with IT, software and analytics knowledge for system configuration, and manufacturing knowledge to communicate with operations teams and validate data. This combination of skills is rare, and such administrators are referred to as 'purple unicorns' because they are not easy to find but in high demand.
c9b1ea545b.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

31e89c19d5.q: How has a small software team remained lean while building a manufacturing platform?
31e89c19d5.a: The founders have 26-plus year careers in B2B software development, which allowed them to build version one themselves and make lean decisions about features. The company focused on inbound marketing rather than heavy sales and marketing staff, rode organic growth and referral networks for nine years, and avoided taking huge investment from private equity or VCs that would force them to chase sales at the expense of business value.
31e89c19d5.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

9f777993a2.q: What is the cost of MES implementation failures in manufacturing environments?
9f777993a2.a: Manufacturing companies are slow to adopt technology because failures carry high risk. If an implementation fails, the likelihood of doing another such project in that company is very low because the company consumes resources, diverts production engineering time, and impacts the bottom line. The failures are more costly in manufacturing than other industries, especially for companies running on thin margins.
9f777993a2.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

ecd3e7363b.q: What measurable inventory improvement resulted from moving from manual paper-based production tracking to automated data collection?
ecd3e7363b.a: One case study with Ice Industries showed effectively zero inventory variance at the end of the year. When operators manually wrote down production totals on paper, they rounded to the expected numbers (e.g., always 1,000 parts per hour), leading to cumulative daily inaccuracies of hundreds of parts. Automated counting down to the stroke and individual part eliminated these discrepancies, improving financial covenants and loan calculations.
ecd3e7363b.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

2dac7c5bb7.q: How much OEE improvement did a food manufacturing company achieve in the first year of implementing production monitoring software?
2dac7c5bb7.a: Louisiana Fish Fry increased their Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) by 12% in the first year. Based on their size and equipment type, this translated to approximately $400,000 a year in savings from increased production when machines were running instead of waiting for repairs.
2dac7c5bb7.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

dba40d4501.q: What role does real-time performance visualization play in engaging manufacturing operators?
dba40d4501.a: Scoreboards displayed on the factory floor show operators their performance with red, yellow, and green indicators against targets. This creates a culture focused on keeping performance green, aligns the entire plant, and engages operators because they understand what they need to do and can see the impact of their actions, leading to better morale and lower turnover.
dba40d4501.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

96e0c874e0.q: How does providing data-driven feedback improve operator engagement and reduce workplace attrition?
96e0c874e0.a: When operators see that management is using data to understand their challenges and act on them, they feel heard and part of the team rather than just a cog in the machine. When supervisors see data showing an operator is struggling with a problem and actively work to fix it, the operator becomes more engaged and feels the company is trying to help, increasing job satisfaction and reducing turnover.
96e0c874e0.e: Podcast episode with Bryan Sapot - CEO, Mingo Smart Factory, and Daniel Langley

752259c94a.q: What is digital maturity and how do manufacturers assess it?
752259c94a.a: Wipfli assesses digital maturity across technology, people, and process through innovation workshops and digital assessments, scoring capabilities in production, quality, and maintenance. They benchmark against a large database called WIPFLY IQ containing data from plastics, molding, and stamping companies, allowing manufacturers to see where they stand compared to similar companies in their industry and revenue range.

2e0d8a3ac7.q: What are the primary technology trends small and medium manufacturers should prioritize?
2e0d8a3ac7.a: Five major trends are industrial machine learning to collect real-time shop floor data, advanced planning and scheduling to improve standards and job profitability, ESG and sustainability activities to reduce carbon footprint, advanced analytics and AI for labor efficiency, and connected worker applications using augmented reality and digital work instructions to reskill people rather than replace them.
2e0d8a3ac7.e: Podcast episode with Mo Abuali - Director, Digital Strategy, Wipfli and Daniel Langley

6c42f43d33.q: What barriers prevent small manufacturers from successfully implementing Industry 4.0 solutions?
6c42f43d33.a: Technology challenges include old IT systems, legacy machines, lack of connectivity and security. Process challenges occur when companies jump to technology without first establishing mature processes, such as implementing predictive maintenance sensors without having a preventive maintenance process in place. People challenges involve change management, requiring friendly user experiences, human-centric machine interfaces, and multidisciplinary teams from operator to C-level to ensure adoption.
6c42f43d33.e: Podcast episode with Mo Abuali - Director, Digital Strategy, Wipfli and Daniel Langley

60d399615e.q: How will industrial AI and generative AI differ in their manufacturing applications over the next five years?
60d399615e.a: Industrial AI and machine learning have existed for decades, using sensor data and machine vision for predictive maintenance, quality tracking, and zero downtime manufacturing. Generative AI, a newer subset powered by deep learning and neural networks, excels at content creation, natural language processing, summarization, and can process multimodal data—text, video, and pictures—through systems like GPT-4 to significantly improve labor efficiency and knowledge transfer.
60d399615e.e: Podcast episode with Mo Abuali - Director, Digital Strategy, Wipfli and Daniel Langley

db0143b151.q: What survey data reveals the gap between digital investment intentions and advanced AI adoption in small manufacturers?
db0143b151.a: Wipfli surveyed approximately 350 small and medium manufacturers across nearly 30 states in North America. The survey found that 99% of respondents prioritize digital investments, but only 30% have started to trial advanced AI solutions, indicating most investments are going into foundational infrastructure—cloud, servers, cybersecurity, networking, and machines—before advancing to AI implementation.
